7954.etyen:
PIE word
 *bʰúHt
Inherited from Old Norse búð (“dwelling; booth, temporary hut”), a variant of Old Norse bóð, from Proto-Germanic *bōþō (“building, hut; dwelling”), a nominal derivative of Proto-Germanic *būaną (“to dwell, reside”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰúHt, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰuH- (“to be, grow”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk bu (“hut, shed”), Icelandic búð, Faroese búð, Swedish bod, Danish bod, German Bude and English booth (“booth, hut; small shop”). / PIE word
 *bʰúHt
Borrowed from Danish bod (“booth, stall; shop”), from Old Danish bōð (“booth, stall”), from Old East Norse bóð (“booth, dwelling”), from Proto-Germanic *bōþō (“building, hut; dwelling”), a nominal derivative of Proto-Germanic *būaną (“to dwell, reside”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰúHt, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰuH- (“to be, grow”).
Compare Swedish bod, German Bude and English booth (“booth, stall; small shop”). / Probably shortened from haugbu (“wight dwelling in a burial mound”), from Old Norse haugbúi (“dweller in a burial mound”). The second element is Old Norse búi (“dweller, inhabitant; farmer”), from Proto-Germanic *būô (“dweller, inhabitant”), ultimately related to the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰuH- (“to be, grow”).
Compare the related inhabitant-forming elements Norwegian Nynorsk -bu, Swedish -bo and Danish -bo (“inhabitant of a place”).

24850.etyen:
Compound of hvitløk (“garlic”) + fedd (“clove”), literally “garlic clove”.
Within the first element, hvit (“white”) continues Old Norse hvítr (“white”), from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz (“white”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweyt- (“to shine”); løk (“onion”) continues Old Norse laukr (“leek, onion, garlic”), from Proto-Germanic *laukaz (“leek, onion”), of uncertain further origin.
The second element comes from Danish fed (“clove; skein”), earlier Danish fid (“skein”); compare Old Norse fit (“hem; webbed foot”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk kvitlaukfedd and Danish hvid

Named after the French explorer Jean-Baptiste Charles Bouvet de Lozier (1705–1786), with øy (“island”) in the feminine definite singular øya (“the island”), literally “the Bouvet island”.
The French surname Bouvet is traditionally derived from Old French bouvet (“young ox”), a diminutive of buef (“ox”) with -et (“diminutive suffix”). buef is from Latin bovem (“ox”), from Proto-Italic *gʷōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws (“cow, ox”). Onomatopoeic, originally imitative of the sound of spitting and subsequently used as an expression of disgust or discomfort.
